item.title: Photo Follow-on Question (7 Years Late)
item.content:encoded:
I stumbled onto this post in late 2019, and wanted to add on to a question asked in the first discussion page. I'm new to the SCP wiki, etc. but have seen enough auto-post responses to know that 'necro-posting' is bad, hence me adding my question here, instead of on the first page as a follow-on to another person's question (I don't think a new post qualifies as a necro, but if I am wrong I apologize in advance).

The original question was where the photos were from - atomicthumbs' answer was "Flickr and Google Images for interesting-looking industrial photos, then processed them to make them look like they came from a 35mm camera loaded with Neopan 1600 film."

The follow-on question from me (even though, 7-almost-8 years have gone by, meaning the answer is probably hard to remember): how were the images processed - Photoshop, some online free tool, something of your own creation, etc.?

I'm very impressed with the quality of the transformation (making a digital photo look like it was scanned from a photo taken on black-and-white film); even a Google image search on the images themselves only returns to the SCP pages, not to any original images (the colored, non-grainy ones). What led to the question is that some of the images I'm curious enough to want to know more about the original image - i.e. is one of them the inside of a clock, an old factory which produced thread, etc.

Thanks for your time - even 7 years later, it's still a very haunting post, turning a somewhat strange but otherwise not that frighting SCP into a horrifying killing zone, made all the more so by the fact that it doesn't intentionally seem to be set-up that way.

item.title: Re: Does this count as necroposting? I have two questions
item.content:encoded:
1. mechano-optical communication- a very cool old-school technology that transmits sound via light without direct use of electricity.
  2. The film canister and sample containers were small enough to fit through the pipe. Support tethers for things like deep-sea operations sometimes have a strand hooked up like a clothesline or flag pole line so that small items can be passed back to the anchor point without the person on the end having to surface, presumably this was the case here.

I think it's the sign of a great SCP that the phrase "Goddamn mice pipe" does absolutely nothing to ruin the tension of the piece.

In regard to the concept, I think it's really cool; exploration logs are some of my favorite articles on the site, and this is one of the best ones out there, if not THE best. Every detail we see just raises more questions about what the hell even is this place, and by the end you have the implication that the universe itself doesn't know, and is just trying to cover it up by killing anyone who goes inside. Very creepy, very impressive.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The log makes this! I'm just outright impressed by the level of humanity displayed. Tropes of the Foundation being ultra-serious and malicious were avoided and outright ignored. I didn't mind the 'cursing', and found it enriching to the experience of the MTF. Anyone offended by the occasional 'bad word' is too soft to be on this site, anyway (Redacted expletives drive me insane, and I'm glad they weren't redacted here). All soldiers use words that sometimes offend soft-minded people, especially when panicked. It's a scientifically proven coping mechanism.

Just some character logic here:

The Foundation cares about its own, and this is an example. We see this in preservation of researchers and MTFs in cases where SCPs are too unpredictable to be handled safely. When Agent Harris goes missing in SCP-1555, they don't leave him for dead. They go hunting for him. The team of course investigates the facility while there, but the mission parameters were to locate the missing agent.

The MTF began their mission with a "Hope for the best, pray for the worst" attitude. These are hardened MTF members with much experience, referencing past mission events as cautionary experiences to avoid mistakes. They go in knowing they're making a risk due to the loss of a previous incursion team member, so right from the start they're on edge. They have the skill to operate, but with no intel on the facility's layout, they were running blind. Panic set in quite quick once the anomalies started pressing in.

I enjoyed the Base operator's tone. He was compassionate and gave careful consideration to morale once he realized there was no chance of them getting out; if I had to die, I'd rather die with hope.

I don't think Shore's ("Delta"'s) superiors would refuse his request, as long as the letter is screened to ensure no classified information is within. It wouldn't be too difficult to give a cover story of his death being the result of combat, or having gone MIA in the deserts of the Middle East or something. For all we know, it could simply be a "sorry for not being there for you" sort of message. The Foundation has no reason to withhold something so innocuous. They do take care of their own.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I love this kind of SCP. It's dangerous and bizarre, and doesn't really make any sense, both in that it defies physics and that it… just doesn't make sense. What's the point of a mouse cannon? It's as if this whole area used to be some kind of huge, secret underground factory of some sort, but the whole section of reality is just… corrupted, somehow. So now it fires mice out of a cannon, rearranges itself, has invisible barriers where the atmosphere suddenly turns to helium or anything passing through gets shredded, and all these other impossible, bizarre things, that don't seem to have been deliberately crafted for any purpose, so much as being corrupted, distorted versions of some ordinary, man-made contraption.

I especially liked the end. Suddenly the tether leads right into a tiny pipe… it's as if the area shifted, but whatever force was responsible for the change made some attempt to preserve the laws of physics and/or the general structure, so rather than the tether suddenly breaking or just leading into a wall, there's a pipe around it. Perhaps the entire place has a defined set of paths, and all that changes is whether those paths are followed by hallways or pipes. Then the tether is somehow growing, and the samples are taking longer than they should to arrive, suggesting some type of time/space anomaly as well. Things are actively stretching and shrinking, by means of mass actually being added and removed.

Everything seems like just weird versions of an otherwise ordinary underground factory. Pipes contain paint, hair, mice… one is "dripping" jars of tree pollen. Again it's as if reality had become corrupted, changing ordinary things into these odd versions. Perhaps this place used to manufacture explosives, but due to the corruption, now makes mice instead… The shifting geometry and occasional changes in both shell composition and content suggest the distortion is ongoing. It does invoke some fear, not in the sense of "this thing is going to kill me" but in just the general feeling of wrongness, that something is broken, something we don't understand, reality itself; and thinking what it'd be like for the explorers inside…

Overall, I found it really enjoyable.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Oddly, I think that's why this bit works. It's not just another "mysterious inscrutable thing that is dangerous…and mysterious…and also inscrutable". We know exactly what it's all for, maybe even a little of how. It's the why that makes no sense, and that's the unnerving bit. Something has created a very elaborate and vast system that exists to do…something, apparently involving a rare species of mouse. We have no idea what that something actually is, though, and the fact that it constantly reconfigures itself seems to suggest it hasn't succeeded at what it's meant to do yet.

I kind of love that.
